questions.question: What is service discovery in microservices architecture?

options.text: A debugging tool for finding bugs in services
A mechanism for services to dynamically find network locations of other services
A process for discovering new features to implement
A database schema discovery tool

questions.explanation: Service discovery enables services to find each other without hardcoded addresses. In dynamic environments like containers and auto-scaling groups, service instances come and go constantly. IP addresses change with every deployment, scale event, or failure recovery. Service discovery provides a way to resolve service names to current network locations. Netflix, Uber, and Airbnb all rely heavily on service discovery to manage thousands of service instances.

questions.question: Why is service discovery essential in microservices and cloud-native environments?

options.text: Services always have static IP addresses that never change
Service instances are dynamic with IPs changing due to scaling, deployments, and failures
It reduces network traffic between services
It is only needed for database connections

questions.explanation: In cloud and container environments, service instances are ephemeral. Auto-scaling adds and removes instances based on load. Deployments replace old instances with new ones. Failures cause instances to restart with new IPs. Container orchestrators like Kubernetes reschedule pods across nodes. Hardcoded IP addresses simply do not work in this environment. Service discovery provides the dynamic resolution that makes microservices possible. Without it, every deployment would require configuration updates across all dependent services.

questions.question: What are the two main service discovery patterns?

options.text: Synchronous and asynchronous discovery
Client-side discovery and server-side discovery
Internal and external discovery
Push-based and pull-based discovery

questions.explanation: Client-side discovery: the client queries the service registry directly, selects an instance using its own load balancing logic, and connects directly to that instance. Server-side discovery: the client calls a load balancer or router, which queries the registry and routes the request to an appropriate instance. Netflix Eureka with Ribbon is client-side. AWS ELB with service registration is server-side. Each pattern has different tradeoffs in complexity, control, and infrastructure requirements.

questions.question: In client-side discovery, what responsibilities does the client have?

options.text: Simply connect to a hardcoded address
Query service registry, select an instance using load balancing logic, and make direct request
Wait passively for the server to initiate connection
Only perform DNS resolution

questions.explanation: Client-side discovery places responsibility on the client: query the registry for available instances, cache the results, apply load balancing logic (round-robin, least connections, random), handle instance failures, and connect directly to the chosen instance. The client has more control over routing decisions but also more complexity. Netflix's Ribbon library implements client-side load balancing. The tradeoff: smarter clients but the discovery logic must be implemented in every client language your organization uses.

questions.question: In server-side discovery, what component routes requests to service instances?

options.text: The client application itself
A load balancer or API gateway that queries the service registry
The database server
A DNS server exclusively

questions.explanation: Server-side discovery uses a load balancer or API gateway as an intermediary. The client only knows the gateway address. The gateway queries the service registry, selects an instance, and routes the request. This simplifies clients (they just call one address) but the gateway becomes a potential bottleneck and single point of failure. AWS Application Load Balancer with ECS service discovery, Kubernetes Services, and Consul Connect all implement server-side discovery patterns.

questions.question: What is a service registry?

options.text: A database storing user registration information
A database of available service instances and their network locations
A source code repository for services
A centralized logging system for services

questions.explanation: The service registry is the central database of service instances: which services exist, their available instances, network locations (IP address and port), health status, and metadata (version, datacenter, tags). Services register on startup and deregister on shutdown. The registry must be highly available because it is a critical dependency for all service communication. Consul, Eureka, etcd, and ZooKeeper are common implementations. Kubernetes uses etcd as its service registry.

questions.question: Which are common service registry implementations? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: HashiCorp Consul
Netflix Eureka
etcd (used by Kubernetes)
MySQL database

questions.explanation: Purpose-built service registries: Consul (HashiCorp, includes service mesh features), Eureka (Netflix OSS, widely used in Spring Cloud), etcd (distributed key-value store, powers Kubernetes service discovery), and ZooKeeper (Apache, used by Kafka and Hadoop). These provide health checking, failure detection, and high availability. MySQL is a general-purpose relational database, not designed for service discovery. It lacks the health checking, watch mechanisms, and consistency guarantees that service registries require.

questions.question: How do services register with the service registry?

options.text: Manual configuration by operators for each deployment
Self-registration on startup or third-party registration by the deployment platform
Automatic detection through network scanning
Email notification to the registry administrator

questions.explanation: Two registration approaches: Self-registration where the service registers itself on startup and sends periodic heartbeats to maintain registration. Third-party registration where the deployment platform (Kubernetes, ECS, Nomad) registers services automatically when they are deployed. Self-registration gives services control but requires registration logic in every service. Third-party registration centralizes the logic but requires platform integration. Kubernetes uses third-party registration through its controller watching pod events.

questions.question: What happens if a service instance crashes without explicitly deregistering from the registry?

options.text: The registry keeps the instance registered forever
Health checks detect the failure and the registry removes the unhealthy instance
All other services crash as well
Nothing happens because crashes are not a problem

questions.explanation: Service registries use health checks to detect failures. Mechanisms include heartbeats (service must send periodic signals), HTTP health endpoints (registry polls /health), and TCP checks (verify port is listening). If an instance stops responding to health checks, it is marked unhealthy and removed from the registry. This handles crashes, network partitions, hung processes, and graceful shutdowns that fail to deregister. Without health checks, crashed instances would receive traffic and cause errors.

questions.question: Can DNS be used for service discovery?

options.text: No, DNS is only for public internet domain resolution
Yes, services can register DNS records and clients resolve service names
No, DNS does not support dynamic updates
Yes, but only for database services

questions.explanation: DNS-based service discovery is possible and widely used. Kubernetes uses CoreDNS to resolve service names to cluster IPs. Consul provides DNS interface alongside its API. Services register DNS records (A records for IPs, SRV records for ports), and clients resolve service names. Limitations: DNS caching can serve stale records after instance changes, TTLs must be short (increasing DNS traffic), and health checking is limited. DNS works well for simpler cases but dedicated registries offer more features.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of client-side discovery over server-side discovery?

options.text: Simpler client implementation with less code
No additional network hop and client can implement custom load balancing strategies
Better security through centralized authentication
Lower infrastructure costs

questions.explanation: Client-side discovery advantages: direct connection to service instances (no gateway hop adding latency), client controls load balancing strategy (can implement custom algorithms based on business logic), and no central bottleneck. The tradeoffs: more complex clients, discovery logic must be implemented in every client language, and clients must handle registry failures. Netflix chose client-side discovery with Eureka and Ribbon because they needed fine-grained control over routing for their complex service mesh.

questions.question: How does Kubernetes handle service discovery?

options.text: It does not support service discovery and requires external tools
Built-in DNS and Service resources that provide stable endpoints for pod groups
External service registry like Consul is always required
Manual IP configuration in deployment manifests

questions.explanation: Kubernetes has built-in service discovery: Service resources provide stable DNS names and virtual IPs (ClusterIP) that do not change even as pods scale. CoreDNS (or kube-dns) resolves service names to ClusterIPs. Endpoints are automatically updated as pods are created and destroyed. Services can be ClusterIP (internal), NodePort (external via node ports), or LoadBalancer (external via cloud LB). No external registry is needed for basic service discovery, though Consul and others can add advanced features.
